tasks.objective: Close the one hole in src/mcp/redact.ts that this epic is guaranteed to walk into: redactText recognises credential SHAPES (sk-, ghp_, xox, JWT, AKIA, Bearer) but has no rule for the shape .env files are made of, so a line like SMTP_LOGIN=hunter2 appearing inside an error message, a parse diagnostic, or anything written to stderr passes through untouched. Every other task in this epic reads .env documents and hands text back to a model, which makes this the leaf that has to land first. The task is deliberately scoped to redact.ts and its test alone — it touches no tool, no manifest and no server wiring — so it is claim-disjoint from task-2-path-guard and the two run concurrently in wave 1. The rule is written to preserve the KEY and destroy the VALUE rather than dropping the whole line, because env_lint's entire product is key names: a redactor that ate the key would make the surface useless, and a redactor that keeps the value makes it dangerous.
acceptance_criteria: redactText('API_TOKEN=sk-live-0123456789abcdef') returns a string that contains 'API_TOKEN', contains the REDACTED marker, and does not contain 'sk-live-0123456789abcdef' — asserted as three separate expectations, because a rule that deleted the whole line would satisfy the third alone.

The non-credential-shaped case is the one that proves the new rule exists: redactText('SMTP_LOGIN=hunter2') does not contain 'hunter2' and does contain 'SMTP_LOGIN'. State the two readings. Under the hypothesis (the .env assignment rule is present) the output is 'SMTP_LOGIN=[redacted]'. Under the null (only the pre-existing SECRET_SHAPED patterns and the SECRET_KEY key-name net exist) the output is the input verbatim, 'SMTP_LOGIN=hunter2' — 'hunter2' matches no token shape and SECRET_KEY never sees it because it is not an object key. The two readings differ in text, so this criterion is not vacuous; the sk-live case above IS vacuous on its own and is retained only for the key-survival half.

redact({ note: 'DB_PASSWORD=hunter2' }) returns { note: 'DB_PASSWORD=[redacted]' } — the new rule reaches values nested inside objects and arrays because redact() already routes every string through redactText. Asserted on a nested structure, not only on a top-level string.
Multiple assignments in one string are all redacted: a two-line string 'A_KEY=one\nB_KEY=two' yields a result containing neither 'one' nor 'two' and containing both 'A_KEY' and 'B_KEY'.
The export prefix does not defeat the rule: redactText('export API_TOKEN=hunter2') does not contain 'hunter2' and does contain 'API_TOKEN'.

Idempotence: for every input in the test table, redactText(redactText(input)) === redactText(input). This is what stops the new rule from chewing on the '[redacted]' marker the shape rules already inserted.

Non-assignments are not touched: redactText('no credentials here') is unchanged, redactError('plain string') is 'plain string', and a string with spaces around the equals sign ('count = 3') is returned unchanged — the rule matches the .env shape KEY=value with no whitespace around the equals sign, not English prose containing an equals sign.
An assignment with an empty value ('EMPTY_KEY=') is returned unchanged: there is nothing to redact and inserting a marker would invent a secret that is not there.

Every test already in test/mcp/redact.test.ts is still present and still green. No existing assertion is deleted, relaxed, or rewritten; the diff to that file is additive apart from imports. A suite that removed an inherited assertion to make the new rule pass is a failed task.
A ReDoS guard test: redactText of a single line consisting of a key, an equals sign and 200,000 value characters completes within Vitest's default timeout and returns a redacted result.

The epic baseline at e0f4266 is 7 files / 187 tests and is a floor, not a target.

functional_clauses: Add exactly one new pattern to redactText: the .env assignment shape. It matches an optional 'export ' prefix, then a key matching [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]{0,127}, then an equals sign with NO whitespace on either side, then a non-empty value run of one or more characters that are not a carriage return or line feed. The match must begin at the start of the string, immediately after a line break, or after whitespace — not in the middle of a word.

The replacement preserves the prefix, the key and the equals sign and replaces only the value run with the existing REDACTED marker: 'API_TOKEN=sk-live-...' becomes 'API_TOKEN=[redacted]'. Do not drop the line, do not drop the key, and do not introduce a second marker constant.

Run the new rule AFTER the existing SECRET_SHAPED patterns in redactText, so an already-substituted marker is the value the new rule sees and replacing it with itself is a no-op. Idempotence is an asserted property, not an assumption.

Over-redaction is the accepted failure direction and is deliberate: a diagnostic containing 'transport=stdio' will come back as 'transport=[redacted]'. Say so in a comment beside the pattern so a later reader does not 'fix' it by loosening the rule. What is not accepted is under-redaction — narrowing the key pattern to UPPER_SNAKE_CASE only, or requiring the value to look credential-shaped, both reopen the exact hole this task closes.

Do not touch the SECRET_KEY key-name net, the existing SECRET_SHAPED array, MAX_DEPTH, the redact() walker, or redactError(). This task adds one pattern and its tests; every other line of redact.ts stays as it is.

Export nothing new from redact.ts. The module's public surface stays REDACTED, redactText, redact and redactError — the tools in the later tasks call redact() and redactError() and must not need to know this rule exists.

tasks.objective: Build src/mcp/paths.ts, the single door through which both new tools read a caller-named file, and cover it with test/mcp/paths.test.ts. The epic's settled design is path-in rather than text-in (MCP-S2: a .env document is a bag of credentials and must never become a tool argument), and path-in is an arbitrary-file-read primitive until it is confined. Confinement therefore ships as its own module, before either tool exists, so it is testable without a protocol client and so exactly one implementation of the rule exists rather than one per tool. The module resolves a caller path against the project root, refuses anything that escapes — traversal, absolute paths, and symlinks whose realpath lands outside — and refuses with the surface's own typed SurfaceError rather than letting a raw fs error out, because an ENOENT string carries an absolute path and that is an information leak of its own. It imports SurfaceError from guard.ts read-only and claims neither guard.ts nor any file task-1-redact-env-shape claims, so the two run concurrently in wave 1.
acceptance_criteria: src/mcp/paths.ts exports PROJECT_ROOT (string), MAX_FILE_BYTES (number), resolveProjectPath(candidate: string, root?: string): string and readProjectFile(candidate: string, root?: string): string. Both functions take the root as an optional second argument defaulting to PROJECT_ROOT, so tests can point them at a temporary directory without any global mutation.

PROJECT_ROOT is derived from import.meta.url exactly as src/mcp/server.ts derives MANIFEST_PATH — two levels up from the module's own directory, so it resolves identically from src/mcp/ and from the built dist/mcp/. A test asserts that PROJECT_ROOT is an absolute path and that resolveProjectPath('mcp.manifest.json') resolves to a file that exists.
Traversal is refused: resolveProjectPath('../../etc/passwd', root) throws SurfaceError with code 'mcp.path-refused'.
Absolute input is refused: resolveProjectPath('/etc/passwd', root) throws SurfaceError with code 'mcp.path-refused'.

The existence-probe criterion, differential. For a root-escaping candidate the refusal must be identical whether or not the target exists. The test resolves two escaping candidates — one naming a file that certainly exists outside the root (a file the test itself creates in a sibling temp directory) and one naming a path that certainly does not — and asserts that the two thrown errors have the same code AND byte-identical message strings. Under the hypothesis (containment is decided lexically, before any filesystem call) both messages are the same fixed refusal text. Under the null (the resolver stats or reads first and maps the fs error) the two messages differ: one reports a readable file or a permission problem, the other carries ENOENT and an absolute path. Different text under the two readings, so the criterion bites.

The prefix-collision criterion: with root <tmp>/envkit and a sibling directory <tmp>/envkit-evil containing a file, resolveProjectPath('../envkit-evil/secret.env', root) throws 'mcp.path-refused'. A containment check written as resolved.startsWith(root) — without requiring a path separator after the root — passes every other escape test in this list and fails this one. That is the whole point of including it.

Symlink escape is refused on the REALPATH, not on the lexical path: a symlink created inside the root whose target is a file outside the root is refused with 'mcp.path-refused' even though its lexical resolution is inside the root.

Symlink probing is refused identically: a dangling symlink inside the root, whose target outside the root does not exist, throws the same code AND the same message as the live symlink in the criterion above. Under the hypothesis (a symlink whose realpath cannot be confirmed inside the root is refused uniformly) both messages are the fixed refusal text. Under the null (realpath failure falls through to an unreadable/ENOENT branch) the dangling case reports a different error than the live case, which lets a caller who can plant a symlink test for the existence of files outside the root.

Symlinks are not banned wholesale — the anti-cheat for the two criteria above: a symlink inside the root pointing at another file inside the root resolves successfully and readProjectFile returns that file's contents. A guard that simply refused every symlink would pass both escape tests and fail this one.

Root normalisation is proven, not assumed: at least one test uses a root created with fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), ...)) and asserts that an ordinary in-root read succeeds. On macOS os.tmpdir() is itself a symlink (/var -> /private/var), so an implementation that compares a realpath'd candidate against a non-realpath'd root refuses its own legitimate files and fails this criterion.

In-root failures are typed, distinct from the escape refusal, and carry no absolute path: a missing file inside the root throws SurfaceError with code 'mcp.path-unreadable'; a directory inside the root throws code 'mcp.path-not-a-file'; a file larger than MAX_FILE_BYTES throws code 'mcp.path-too-large'. A test asserts for each of the four codes that the message contains neither the string PROJECT_ROOT resolves to, nor the substring 'ENOENT', 'EISDIR', 'EACCES' or 'EPERM'.

Degenerate input is refused rather than crashing: an empty string, a whitespace-only string, a string containing a NUL character, and a candidate longer than 1024 characters each throw a SurfaceError (not a TypeError, not a raw Error from node:path) — asserted for each.

readProjectFile decodes UTF-8 and never throws for byte content that is not valid UTF-8: a test writes a file of arbitrary bytes inside the root and asserts readProjectFile returns a string rather than throwing.
MAX_FILE_BYTES is 1048576 (1 MiB) and the size is checked from a stat BEFORE the file is read into memory — a test on a file just over the cap asserts 'mcp.path-too-large'.
src/mcp/paths.ts imports only node:fs, node:path, node:url and ./guard.js. No npm package, no other project module.
src/mcp/guard.ts is byte-identical to its state at the start of the task — SurfaceError is imported, never edited, and no new export is added to guard.ts.

functional_clauses: Order of operations in resolveProjectPath, and it is load-bearing: (1) validate the candidate is a non-empty string under 1024 characters with no NUL byte; (2) compute realRoot = fs.realpathSync(path.resolve(root)) once, so a symlinked root such as macOS's /var/folders temp path is compared like for like; (3) compute resolved = path.resolve(realRoot, candidate); (4) decide containment LEXICALLY — resolved === realRoot || resolved.startsWith(realRoot + path.sep) — and throw 'mcp.path-refused' here, before any stat, read or realpath of the candidate; (5) only then touch the filesystem. Steps 4 and 5 must not be reordered: doing any filesystem work before the containment decision is what turns the refusal into an existence oracle.

Containment must compare whole path segments. resolved.startsWith(realRoot) alone is wrong because '<tmp>/envkit-evil/x' starts with '<tmp>/envkit'; require equality with the root or a path.sep immediately after it.

After containment passes, resolve symlinks: call fs.realpathSync on the resolved path. If it succeeds and the result is not contained by realRoot under the same whole-segment rule, throw 'mcp.path-refused' with the SAME message used in step 4. If it throws ENOENT and fs.lstatSync reports the entry itself is a symlink, throw 'mcp.path-refused' with that same message — a dangling symlink's target is unverifiable, and an unverifiable target is refused, not reported as missing.

If the entry is not a symlink and does not exist, throw 'mcp.path-unreadable'. If it exists and is not a regular file, throw 'mcp.path-not-a-file'. If its size exceeds MAX_FILE_BYTES, throw 'mcp.path-too-large'. Any other filesystem error (EACCES, EPERM, EMFILE, anything) is caught and rethrown as 'mcp.path-unreadable' — no raw fs error, no errno string and no absolute path ever leaves this module.

Every message this module emits may name the caller's own relative candidate string and nothing else. It must never contain the project root, an absolute path, a realpath, an errno code, or any statement about what does or does not exist outside the root. The caller already knows what it asked for; it must learn nothing else.

The refusal for anything outside the root is exactly one fixed sentence, produced from one string constant, so the two differential criteria compare identical text rather than similar text. Do not interpolate the resolved path, the reason, or the failing step into it.

readProjectFile(candidate, root) = resolveProjectPath then fs.readFileSync(resolved, 'utf8'). It performs no parsing, no trimming and no normalisation of the content — it returns the document as text for parseEnv to handle.

Throw the SurfaceError class imported from ./guard.js. Do not define a second error class, do not subclass it, and do not add these codes to guard.ts — guard.ts is out of claim and the codes belong with the module that raises them.

The root is never taken from a tool argument, from process.cwd(), from process.env, or from any client-controlled value. It is PROJECT_ROOT by default and an explicit in-process function argument otherwise. The strings 'process.cwd' and 'process.env' must not appear in src/mcp/paths.ts at all — grep the diff.

Stateless: no module-level cache of resolved paths, stat results or file contents. Two identical calls do the same filesystem work twice (MCP-P3: nothing survives a reconnect because nothing is kept).

Inside src/mcp/, only those two packages and Node builtins may be imported; this module needs only builtins and ./guard.js. A third runtime dependency is an operator question, never a coder decision.

No task in this epic may reduce envkit's existing gates (baseline e0f4266: 7 test files, 187 tests, all four gates green). Deleting, skipping or weakening an existing test to get green is a failed task.

This module is the epic's security boundary. It fails closed: any condition it did not anticipate ends in a typed refusal, never in a successful read and never in an uncaught exception. Argue every branch to a throw or a return; there is no default fall-through.

No TOCTOU widening: do the containment decision and the read against the same resolved path within one call, and never re-derive the path from the candidate a second time. A perfectly race-free check is out of scope for a stdio server reading local files — say so in a comment rather than pretending otherwise.

Totality on input: resolveProjectPath and readProjectFile must not throw anything other than SurfaceError, for any string candidate and any root. Enforced by a hostile-input table test covering at least the empty string, whitespace, NUL, an over-long path, '.', '..', a path of many '../' segments, a path with embedded newlines, and a path that is a bare '/'.

Secret hygiene: this module never logs, never writes to stdout or stderr, and never puts file CONTENT into an error message. A test asserts that reading a file whose content is 'API_TOKEN=s3cr3t-value' and then triggering a size or type failure on a neighbouring path produces no message containing 's3cr3t-value'.
stdout belongs to the protocol: no console.log, console.info, console.warn or process.stdout.write anywhere under src/mcp/.
No eval, no new Function, no dynamic import(), no child processes, no network. The module reads files and resolves paths; that is all it does.

Tests create every fixture under a fresh fs.mkdtempSync directory and remove it in a cleanup hook. No fixture file is committed. In particular no file named .env or .env.* may be added to the repo: .gitignore ignores both patterns, so such a fixture would pass locally and vanish in CI — a test that is green because its input is untracked is a test that proves nothing.

TDD is gate-enforced: the failing test exists before the implementation that makes it pass. Tests assert observable behaviour — thrown codes, thrown messages, returned strings — never internal helper names.

Strict YAGNI: implement resolveProjectPath, readProjectFile and the two constants. No glob support, no directory listing, no write path, no caching layer, no allowlist of extensions, no configurable root registry, no async variants. A directory-listing helper in particular is a new arbitrary-read primitive and is out of scope.
English-only code, comments and commit messages; formatting is exactly what the committed Biome config produces, with zero rule suppressions.

Do not create, modify or delete any file outside src/mcp/paths.ts and test/mcp/paths.test.ts — in particular not src/mcp/guard.ts (import from it, never edit it), src/mcp/redact.ts, src/mcp/server.ts, mcp.manifest.json, package.json or any config file. Out-of-claim edits fail the gate.

tasks.objective: Ship env_lint end to end in one task: the manifest declaration, the tool implementation, its registration in server.ts, and the surface-test case an agent's view is asserted from. It is one task and not three because test/mcp/surface.test.ts asserts that tools/list equals manifest.tools exactly — a task that declared the tool without registering it would turn that existing test red, and a task that registered without declaring would throw mcp.undeclared-tool out of guard.ts before connect(). Manifest and registration are therefore the same atomic unit; the gate scores the worktree's final state, so the invariant holds at every commit boundary rather than being repaired by a follow-up. env_lint takes a project-relative PATH, not the document text, because a .env document is a bag of credentials and MCP-S2 forbids credentials arriving as arguments; it reads through task-2-path-guard's readProjectFile so the path-in shape is confined, and it parses with envkit's own parseEnv so no new dependency and no second parser enter the project. Its output is key NAMES and issue metadata — never a value, not truncated, not hashed. This task also adds the projectRoot injection point to buildServer that the surface test needs to point a real server at a temporary fixture directory; task-4-env-diff-keys reuses it. Because it claims mcp.manifest.json, src/mcp/server.ts and test/mcp/surface.test.ts, it is serialized against task-4-env-diff-keys by a claim-order edge.
acceptance_criteria: mcp.manifest.json declares a second tool named exactly 'env_lint' with mutation 'read-only' and annotations readOnlyHint: true, destructiveHint: false, idempotentHint: true, openWorldHint: false, plus a title and a description. No 'approval' block is added and no non-read-only tool is declared anywhere in this diff.
mcp.manifest.json's version is bumped from '0.0.0' to '0.1.0' — MCP-P2: clients cache a tool surface against the version, so a surface change is a version bump. It stays valid semver.

A new test in test/mcp/surface.test.ts asserts the manifest-policy facts a reviewer would otherwise have to eyeball: every entry in manifest.tools has a name matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,63}$, names are unique, every entry declares mutation 'read-only', and every read-only entry annotates readOnlyHint true / destructiveHint false / openWorldHint false. This is the in-worktree stand-in for `smith mcp check`. That command can be pointed at a worktree (`--target-dir`, cli.ts:787), but its exit code also folds in the roadmap verdict MCP-M2, which stays red until the operator closes the envkit-mcp-surface milestone at epic close. So no coder can make it exit 0, and a gate a worker cannot satisfy is not a gate a worker should be graded on.

src/mcp/tools/env-lint.ts exports registerEnvLintTool(server, manifest, options) and calls requireDeclaredTool(manifest, 'env_lint', 'read-only') before registering anything, following the six-step recipe in src/mcp/README.md.

The tool declares a zod input schema of exactly one property: path, a string, required, with a description and a max length of 1024. MCP-P4. A surface test calls env_lint with { path: 42 } and asserts isError is true; another calls it with {} and asserts isError is true.
The tool takes NO text, content, document, body or data parameter under any name. Mechanically checkable: the input schema object in src/mcp/tools/env-lint.ts has exactly one key, and it is 'path'.

Happy path through a real client over the in-memory transport: given a fixture file inside a temporary project root containing 'API_TOKEN=sk-live-0123456789abcdef', 'SMTP_LOGIN=hunter2' and 'DEBUG=true', the response payload lists the key names API_TOKEN, SMTP_LOGIN and DEBUG.

The secret criterion, and it is differential: the same response's full text contains neither 'sk-live-0123456789abcdef' nor 'hunter2'. Under the hypothesis (the tool projects Object.keys(parseEnv(text).values) and never carries a value) the payload holds three key names and no value at all. Under the null (the tool returns the values map and leans on redact() to clean it) 'sk-live-0123456789abcdef' would still be scrubbed by the SECRET_SHAPED net, but 'hunter2' would survive verbatim: SMTP_LOGIN matches no SECRET_KEY pattern and 'hunter2' matches no token shape. The two readings differ in text on the SMTP_LOGIN line, which is what makes this criterion a test of the projection rather than a test of the redactor.

Parse issues are reported with code, 1-based line and message and nothing else: a fixture whose malformed line is 'this line has no equals sign s3cr3t-value' produces an issue array of length 1 whose entry has the code parseEnv assigns and whose message does not contain 's3cr3t-value'.

The payload never contains an absolute path: the response text does not contain the temporary root's absolute path, and the echoed path field is byte-identical to the relative string the caller supplied.

Refusal is typed and mute, asserted through the protocol: calling env_lint with path '../../etc/passwd' returns isError true with text naming the code 'mcp.path-refused', containing no absolute path and no 'ENOENT'. Calling it with a path that escapes the root and certainly does not exist returns byte-identical text. Under the hypothesis (paths.ts decides containment before touching the filesystem and the tool passes its message through redactError) the two error texts are identical. Under the null (the tool catches and formats the underlying fs error) they differ, and the difference tells a caller whether /etc/passwd exists on the host.

A path inside the root that does not exist returns isError true naming 'mcp.path-unreadable' — distinguishable from the escape refusal, which is correct: the caller is entitled to know that a file it is allowed to read is missing, and entitled to know nothing about anything outside the root.

The tool never throws out of its handler: a table test drives at least six hostile path arguments (empty string, '.', '..', a 2000-character path, a path containing a NUL character, a path with a newline) through a real client and asserts every call returns a result — isError true is fine, an unhandled rejection or a closed transport is not.

functional_clauses: Order of operations in resolveProjectPath, and it is load-bearing: (1) validate the candidate is a non-empty string under 1024 characters with no NUL byte; (2) compute realRoot = fs.realpathSync(path.resolve(root)) once, so a symlinked root such as macOS's /var/folders temp path is compared like for like; (3) compute resolved = path.resolve(realRoot, candidate); (4) decide containment LEXICALLY — resolved === realRoot || resolved.startsWith(realRoot + path.sep) — and throw 'mcp.path-refused' here, before any stat, read or realpath of the candidate; (5) only then touch the filesystem. Steps 4 and 5 must not be reordered: doing any filesystem work before the containment decision is what turns the refusal into an existence oracle.

Containment must compare whole path segments. resolved.startsWith(realRoot) alone is wrong because '<tmp>/envkit-evil/x' starts with '<tmp>/envkit'; require equality with the root or a path.sep immediately after it.

After containment passes, resolve symlinks: call fs.realpathSync on the resolved path. If it succeeds and the result is not contained by realRoot under the same whole-segment rule, throw 'mcp.path-refused' with the SAME message used in step 4. If it throws ENOENT and fs.lstatSync reports the entry itself is a symlink, throw 'mcp.path-refused' with that same message — a dangling symlink's target is unverifiable, and an unverifiable target is refused, not reported as missing.

If the entry is not a symlink and does not exist, throw 'mcp.path-unreadable'. If it exists and is not a regular file, throw 'mcp.path-not-a-file'. If its size exceeds MAX_FILE_BYTES, throw 'mcp.path-too-large'. Any other filesystem error (EACCES, EPERM, EMFILE, anything) is caught and rethrown as 'mcp.path-unreadable' — no raw fs error, no errno string and no absolute path ever leaves this module.

Every message this module emits may name the caller's own relative candidate string and nothing else. It must never contain the project root, an absolute path, a realpath, an errno code, or any statement about what does or does not exist outside the root. The caller already knows what it asked for; it must learn nothing else.

The refusal for anything outside the root is exactly one fixed sentence, produced from one string constant, so the two differential criteria compare identical text rather than similar text. Do not interpolate the resolved path, the reason, or the failing step into it.

readProjectFile(candidate, root) = resolveProjectPath then fs.readFileSync(resolved, 'utf8'). It performs no parsing, no trimming and no normalisation of the content — it returns the document as text for parseEnv to handle.

tasks.objective: Build src/mcp/paths.ts, the single door through which both new tools read a caller-named file, and cover it with test/mcp/paths.test.ts. The epic's settled design is path-in rather than text-in (MCP-S2: a .env document is a bag of credentials and must never become a tool argument), and path-in is an arbitrary-file-read primitive until it is confined. Confinement therefore ships as its own module, before either tool exists, so it is testable without a protocol client and so exactly one implementation of the rule exists rather than one per tool. The module resolves a caller path against the project root, refuses anything that escapes — traversal, absolute paths, and symlinks whose realpath lands outside — and refuses with the surface's own typed SurfaceError rather than letting a raw fs error out, because an ENOENT string carries an absolute path and that is an information leak of its own. It imports SurfaceError from guard.ts read-only and claims neither guard.ts nor any file task-1-redact-env-shape claims, so the two run concurrently in wave 1.
acceptance_criteria: src/mcp/paths.ts exports PROJECT_ROOT (string), MAX_FILE_BYTES (number), resolveProjectPath(candidate: string, root?: string): string and readProjectFile(candidate: string, root?: string): string. Both functions take the root as an optional second argument defaulting to PROJECT_ROOT, so tests can point them at a temporary directory without any global mutation.

PROJECT_ROOT is derived from import.meta.url exactly as src/mcp/server.ts derives MANIFEST_PATH — two levels up from the module's own directory, so it resolves identically from src/mcp/ and from the built dist/mcp/. A test asserts that PROJECT_ROOT is an absolute path and that resolveProjectPath('mcp.manifest.json') resolves to a file that exists.
Traversal is refused: resolveProjectPath('../../etc/passwd', root) throws SurfaceError with code 'mcp.path-refused'.
Absolute input is refused: resolveProjectPath('/etc/passwd', root) throws SurfaceError with code 'mcp.path-refused'.

The existence-probe criterion, differential. For a root-escaping candidate the refusal must be identical whether or not the target exists. The test resolves two escaping candidates — one naming a file that certainly exists outside the root (a file the test itself creates in a sibling temp directory) and one naming a path that certainly does not — and asserts that the two thrown errors have the same code AND byte-identical message strings. Under the hypothesis (containment is decided lexically, before any filesystem call) both messages are the same fixed refusal text. Under the null (the resolver stats or reads first and maps the fs error) the two messages differ: one reports a readable file or a permission problem, the other carries ENOENT and an absolute path. Different text under the two readings, so the criterion bites.

The prefix-collision criterion: with root <tmp>/envkit and a sibling directory <tmp>/envkit-evil containing a file, resolveProjectPath('../envkit-evil/secret.env', root) throws 'mcp.path-refused'. A containment check written as resolved.startsWith(root) — without requiring a path separator after the root — passes every other escape test in this list and fails this one. That is the whole point of including it.

Symlink escape is refused on the REALPATH, not on the lexical path, at EVERY depth — the final component and any ancestor directory. (a) A symlink inside the root whose target is a file outside the root is refused with 'mcp.path-refused' even though its lexical resolution is inside the root. (b) A symlinked DIRECTORY inside the root whose target is a directory outside it: with root/link -> <tmp>/outside and <tmp>/outside/exists.txt present, resolveProjectPath('link/exists.txt', root) throws 'mcp.path-refused'. (c) The oracle differential for (b), which is the half v3 had no criterion for at all: resolveProjectPath('link/missing.txt', root) — same escaping ancestor, target absent — throws the SAME code AND a byte-identical message to (b). Under the hypothesis (containment is re-decided on the deepest existing ancestor's realpath, functional_clauses[2] branch b) both are the fixed refusal text. Under the null (only the final component is examined for symlink-ness, which is what v3's contract literally described) (b) is refused by the realpath-success branch and (c) falls through to 'mcp.path-unreadable' — and that difference lets a caller who can plant one directory symlink test the existence of any file anywhere outside the root. Two tests for this case already exist in the shipped test/mcp/paths.test.ts, added by a fix commit and traceable to no criterion in v3, so nothing would have caught a refactor that dropped them (spec finding f-envkit-mcp-surface/integration-b029d293). This criterion is what they answer to.

Symlink probing is refused identically, and an in-root malformation is NOT reported as an escape. (a) A dangling symlink inside the root, whose target outside the root does not exist, throws the same code AND the same message as the live escaping symlink in the criterion above. Under the hypothesis (a symlink whose realpath cannot be confirmed inside the root is refused uniformly) both messages are the fixed refusal text. Under the null (realpath failure falls through to an unreadable/ENOENT branch) the dangling case reports a different error than the live case, which lets a caller who can plant a symlink test for the existence of files outside the root. (b) The converse, which v3 specified in neither direction: a symlink cycle wholly INSIDE the root (root/a -> root/b and root/b -> root/a, so realpathSync throws ELOOP and neither entry ever leaves the root) throws 'mcp.path-unreadable', not 'mcp.path-refused'. Under the hypothesis (the catch branches on the errno and the ancestor walk finds no escape) the caller is told the entry is unreadable, which is true. Under the null (any realpath failure on a symlink is refused, which is what the shipped src/mcp/paths.ts does) the caller is told the path is outside the project, which is false (spec finding f-envkit-mcp-surface/integration-8248d134). Safe in both readings — it fails closed and leaks nothing — but only one of them is accurate about why. The message for (b) still carries no absolute path and no errno string, per AC[10].

Symlinks are not banned wholesale — the anti-cheat for the two criteria above: a symlink inside the root pointing at another file inside the root resolves successfully and readProjectFile returns that file's contents. A guard that simply refused every symlink would pass both escape tests and fail this one.

Root normalisation is proven, not assumed: at least one test uses a root created with fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), ...)) and asserts that an ordinary in-root read succeeds. On macOS os.tmpdir() is itself a symlink (/var -> /private/var), so an implementation that compares a realpath'd candidate against a non-realpath'd root refuses its own legitimate files and fails this criterion.

In-root failures are typed, distinct from the escape refusal, and carry no absolute path: a missing file inside the root throws SurfaceError with code 'mcp.path-unreadable'; a directory inside the root throws code 'mcp.path-not-a-file'; a file larger than MAX_FILE_BYTES throws code 'mcp.path-too-large'. A test asserts for each of the four codes that the message contains neither the string PROJECT_ROOT resolves to, nor the substring 'ENOENT', 'EISDIR', 'EACCES' or 'EPERM'.

Degenerate input is refused rather than crashing: an empty string, a whitespace-only string, a string containing a NUL character, and a candidate longer than 1024 characters each throw a SurfaceError (not a TypeError, not a raw Error from node:path) — asserted for each.

readProjectFile decodes UTF-8 and never throws for byte content that is not valid UTF-8: a test writes a file of arbitrary bytes inside the root and asserts readProjectFile returns a string rather than throwing.
MAX_FILE_BYTES is 1048576 (1 MiB) and the size is checked from a stat BEFORE the file is read into memory — a test on a file just over the cap asserts 'mcp.path-too-large'.

functional_clauses: Order of operations in resolveProjectPath, and it is load-bearing: (1) validate the candidate is a non-empty string under 1024 characters with no NUL byte; (2) compute realRoot = fs.realpathSync(path.resolve(root)) once, so a symlinked root such as macOS's /var/folders temp path is compared like for like; (3) compute resolved = path.resolve(realRoot, candidate); (4) decide containment LEXICALLY — resolved === realRoot || resolved.startsWith(realRoot + path.sep) — and throw 'mcp.path-refused' here, before any stat, read or realpath of the candidate; (5) only then touch the filesystem. Steps 4 and 5 must not be reordered: doing any filesystem work before the containment decision is what turns the refusal into an existence oracle.

Containment must compare whole path segments. resolved.startsWith(realRoot) alone is wrong because '<tmp>/envkit-evil/x' starts with '<tmp>/envkit'; require equality with the root or a path.sep immediately after it.

After containment passes, resolve symlinks: call fs.realpathSync on the resolved path. If it succeeds and the result is not contained by realRoot under the same whole-segment rule, throw 'mcp.path-refused' with the SAME message used in step 4. If it throws, branch on why — v3's clause named only ENOENT and left every other failure undefined, and the shipped code branched on none of them. (a) The entry itself is a symlink (fs.lstatSync reports one) and the failure is ENOENT: throw 'mcp.path-refused' with that same message — a dangling symlink's target is unverifiable, and an unverifiable target is refused, not reported as missing. (b) The entry does not exist, symlink or not: walk UP from the resolved path to its deepest EXISTING ancestor, realpath that ancestor, and apply the same whole-segment containment rule to the result; if the ancestor's realpath escapes realRoot, throw 'mcp.path-refused' with that same message. This branch is not an implementation detail and not optional. Without it, root/link -> /outside makes 'link/exists.txt' refused by the success branch while 'link/missing.txt' falls through to 'mcp.path-unreadable', and the difference between those two answers is an existence oracle for the far side of the symlink — the same oracle AC[4] and AC[7] close one path segment lower down (spec finding f-envkit-mcp-surface/integration-b029d293). The walk terminates at realRoot, which exists by step 2. (c) Any other failure — ELOOP from a symlink cycle, EACCES on an intermediate directory — with no escape found by (b): this is an in-root-only failure, typed per clause 4. Do not reuse the escape refusal for it.

If the entry is not a symlink and does not exist, throw 'mcp.path-unreadable'. A malformed entry that never LEAVES the root is 'mcp.path-unreadable' too, not 'mcp.path-refused': a symlink cycle inside the root (ELOOP), an unreadable intermediate directory (EACCES). The escape refusal is one fixed sentence saying the path is outside the project, and for an in-root loop that sentence is simply false (spec finding f-envkit-mcp-surface/integration-8248d134). It fails closed either way and leaks nothing; the defect is that it misreports why, and a message that lies about the reason is one a future reader will act on. If it exists and is not a regular file, throw 'mcp.path-not-a-file'. If its size exceeds MAX_FILE_BYTES, throw 'mcp.path-too-large'. Any other filesystem error (EACCES, EPERM, EMFILE, anything) is caught and rethrown as 'mcp.path-unreadable' — no raw fs error, no errno string and no absolute path ever leaves this module.

Every message this module emits may name the caller's own relative candidate string and nothing else. It must never contain the project root, an absolute path, a realpath, an errno code, or any statement about what does or does not exist outside the root. The caller already knows what it asked for; it must learn nothing else.

The refusal for anything outside the root is exactly one fixed sentence, produced from one string constant, so the two differential criteria compare identical text rather than similar text. Do not interpolate the resolved path, the reason, or the failing step into it.

readProjectFile(candidate, root) = resolveProjectPath then fs.readFileSync(resolved, 'utf8'). It performs no parsing, no trimming and no normalisation of the content — it returns the document as text for parseEnv to handle.

Throw the SurfaceError class imported from ./guard.js. Do not define a second error class, do not subclass it, and do not add these codes to guard.ts — guard.ts is out of claim and the codes belong with the module that raises them.

The root is never taken from a tool argument, from process.cwd(), from process.env, or from any client-controlled value. It is PROJECT_ROOT by default and an explicit in-process function argument otherwise. The strings 'process.cwd' and 'process.env' must not appear in src/mcp/paths.ts at all — grep the diff.
